title: The terminal and first steps
lead: Learn to read the prompt, type your first commands and find help when you get stuck.
objectives: You can read the user, machine and directory shown in the prompt.
You run safe first commands such as whoami, hostname, pwd and ls.
You find help yourself with man, --help and error messages.

sections.title: Terminal and prompt
body: The **terminal** is the window where you give the computer text commands. The program running inside it is the **shell**; the most common one is `bash`. The shell reads your line, runs it and prints the result.

The **prompt** at the start of each line tells you three things: who you are, which machine you are on and which directory you are in. Example: `student@linux-lab:~$` — user `student`, machine `linux-lab`, `~` means the home directory. A trailing `$` marks a normal user, `#` marks the administrator (root).
sections.tip: Nothing runs until you press Enter. Use Backspace to fix typos.

sections.title: First commands: who am I, where am I?
body: Before touching a system you must know who you are and where you are. The commands below only read information and change nothing. Click a box to paste the command into the terminal.

commands.what: Prints the user you are working as.
commands.where: After login, and before and after using sudo.
commands.why: Prevents actions with the wrong user.

commands.where: When you connect to several servers.
commands.why: Makes sure you are on the right machine.

commands.what: Prints the full path of the current directory.
commands.why: Knowing your location prevents mistakes in file operations.

commands.what: Lists files and folders in the current directory. -l adds details.
Prints the text you give it and expands variables like $USER.
commands.where: In scripts and for quick experiments.
commands.why: The simplest way to see a variable's value.

sections.title: Getting help and reading errors
body: Every Linux command has a manual: `man command` shows it in full, `command --help` shows a short summary. If you type an unknown command the shell says `command not found` — that is information, not a disaster: you probably made a typo.
The shell also saves time: **Tab** completes commands and file names, **↑ / ↓** recalls earlier commands, `history` lists them all with numbers, `clear` wipes the screen.

commands.where: When you want to look up a command's options.
commands.why: You get the right information straight from your own system.
Shorter than man and often enough.

commands.where: To find an old command again.
commands.why: You don't have to retype everything.

sections.tip: Pressing Tab twice lists all possible completions. Try typing `whoa` and press Tab.

t01.text: Type `whoami` and read which user you are working as.
t01.hint: Just type the command name and press Enter.

t02.text: Use `hostname` to find the machine's name.
t02.hint: The output matches the word after the @ in the prompt.

t03.text: Use `pwd` to print the full path of the current directory.
t03.hint: The path starts with / — an absolute path.

t04.hint: Put the text inside double quotes.

t05.text: List the directory in detail with `ls -l`. What does the `d` in the first column mean?
t05.hint: d means directory, - means a regular file.

t06.text: Open the manual of `ls` with `man ls`.

t08.text: Deliberately type a command that does not exist (e.g. `lss`) and read the error.
t08.hint: The message is command not found — a sign of a typo.

t09.text: Show the running kernel version with `uname -r`.

t10.text: Type `echo $USER`. Is the output the same as `whoami`?
t10.hint: The dollar sign expands the variable to its value.

t11.text: Run in order: `pwd`, `ls`, `cd Documents`, `pwd`. How did your location change?
t11.hint: Four separate lines, each with Enter.

t12.text: List the commands you typed in this session with `history`.

t14.text: Challenge: in your home directory create a file with `echo Hello > first.txt`, then read it with `cat first.txt`.
t14.hint: The > writes output into a file. First return home with `cd ~`.

t15.text: Predict: `cd ~/Documents`, then `cd ..`, then `pwd`. Predict which path you will see before running it, then check.

t16.text: Debug: a colleague typed `cat nots.txt` and got an error. Find the correct name with `ls` in your home directory and read the file with `cat`.
t16.hint: A misspelled file name gives 'No such file'; use the name from the `ls` output.

t17.text: Mini project: write your user name into a file with `whoami > hello.txt`, then read it with `cat hello.txt`.
t17.hint: `>` redirects output into a file. `cd ~` first.

t18.text: TICKET #1001 — Support needs system info: in your home directory write the kernel version (`uname -r`) and then the host name (`hostname`) into `info.txt`. The file must have 2 lines.
t18.hint: Use `>` for the first and `>>` (append) for the second; otherwise the first line is lost.

q1.q: Your prompt ends with `#`. What does that mean?
options: The command was written as a comment
You are working as the administrator (root)
q1.explain: `$` means a normal user, `#` means root. A wrong command as root can do great damage — be careful.

q2.q: How do you open a command's manual?
q2.explain: `man command` opens the full manual; `command --help` gives a short summary.

q3.q: What does `command not found` usually mean?
options: The command name is misspelled or the command is not installed
q3.explain: Check the spelling first; then check whether the command is installed.

q4.q: Which key completes a partly typed command or file name?
q4.explain: Tab completes; pressed twice it lists the options.

summary: The prompt shows user, machine and directory; `$` is normal, `#` is root.
For help use `man command` and `command --help`; error messages are clues.

glossary.meaning: The window where you type commands.
The program that runs your commands, e.g. bash.
The user@machine:directory info at the start of each line.
The user's own folder, written as ~.

vm.intro: Do the tasks below on your own Linux VM (Rocky/Alma or Ubuntu). If you do not have a VM yet, see module 0.2 first.

v01.title: Find your kernel version
v01.text: Open a terminal in your VM and print the version of the running kernel. Paste the output below.
differs: Your version number may differ; what matters is a dotted version such as `5.14.0`.
If you see `command not found`, check spelling (lower case, spaces).

v02.title: Identify your distribution
v02.text: The file `/etc/os-release` tells you the distribution name and version.
differs: On Ubuntu you will see `NAME="Ubuntu"`; that is normal.
On `No such file` make sure you are on a real distribution, not a bare container.

v03.title: Your first file
v03.text: Write and read a file in your home directory. The output must contain `Hello`; then press "Done".

blocks.cmd: cd ~ && echo Hello > first.txt && cat first.txt

differs: If nothing shows, check with `ls -l first.txt` that the file was created.
